We need to cluster equivalent facts. Let's list each candidate meaning.

0: photosynthesis occurs in chloroplast (process in organelle). 8: photosynthesis process occurs in chloroplasts (plural). 18: photosynthesis process location chloroplasts (relation "location"). Are these equivalent? Relation "occurs in" vs "location". Likely same proposition: process occurs in organelle. The paragraph says "photosynthesis process in chloroplasts begins...". So 0,8,18 are essentially same. Need check if any nuance: 0 uses "occurs in", 8 same, 18 uses "location". According to rules, synonyms of relation allowed if same meaning. So they are duplicates. All three can be grouped.

Check also any other similar: maybe none.

1: electron of P680 of PSII energy level higher (relation "energy level" object "higher"). 9: electron of P680 of PSII attains higher energy level (relation attains). 19 duplicate of 9 (same). 1 is different phrasing: relation "energy level" vs "attains". Does that convey same complete proposition? 1 says "energy level" is higher. 9 says "attains higher energy level". Both assert that the electron has a higher energy level. Are they equivalent? The paragraph: "when an electron of P680 of PSII attains a higher - energy level." So 9 matches. 1 says "energy level higher". That's essentially same assertion that the electron's energy level is higher. The relation difference but meaning same. According to allowed synonyms, "energy level" as relation maybe not standard but conveys same. I'd consider them equivalent. However need check if 1 missing "attains" action vs state. 1 says "energy level" is higher (a property). 9 says it attains higher energy level (event). Slight nuance: one is a state, other is an event of attaining. The paragraph describes the process of attaining. 1 could be interpreted as the electron's energy level is higher (maybe after attainment). Might be considered equivalent? The test: could one be true while other false? If electron has higher energy level, then it must have attained it? Possibly yes, but could be higher without attains? In context, they refer to the moment of attaining. I'd err to keep separate because one is about the event of attaining, other about the state. The rule says keep different events separate. So keep separate groups.

Thus group for 9 and 19 (identical). 1 separate.

2: chain of electron acceptors named as electron transport chain. 13: chain of electron acceptors has name electron transport chain. 22: chain of electron acceptors also known as electron transport chain. All same meaning. So group 2,13,22.

3: electron state excited condition when chain reaches PS I. 4: electron redox potential high condition when chain reaches PS I. 15: electron becomes excited high redox potential (no condition). 24: electron creates high redox potential (no condition). Need evaluate equivalence.

3 says electron is excited (state) when chain reaches PS I. 4 says electron redox potential high when chain reaches PS I. These are different properties (state vs redox potential). Not equivalent.

15 says electron becomes excited, high redox potential (object "high redox potential") maybe conflates both? Actually relation "becomes excited", object "high redox potential". That's odd: mixing. Might be considered same as 3+4 combined? But 15 says becomes excited, high redox potential (maybe both). The paragraph: "When this chain reaches PS I, an electron is again excited, creating a high redox - potential." So there are two statements: electron excited, and creates high redox potential. 3 captures excited with condition. 4 captures high redox potential with condition. 15 captures both in one statement (becomes excited, high redox potential) without condition. Not equivalent because missing condition. So separate.

24: electron creates high redox potential (no condition). Equivalent to 4? 4 includes condition "when chain reaches PS I". So not equivalent.

Thus keep 3 separate, 4 separate, 15 separate, 24 separate.

5: electron transport chain of photosynthesis depicted in z-scheme. 16 duplicate (same). 25 duplicate but object "z - scheme" with spaces. All same. So group 5,16,25.

6: z-scheme named after letter Z. 7: redox diagram from P680 to P700 resembles letter Z. 17 similar but object type character. 26: redox diagram resembles letter z with start/end qualifiers. Are these equivalent? 6 says naming origin. 7 says diagram resembles letter Z (the reason for name). 17 same. 26 also says resembles letter z with start/end qualifiers. All convey that the redox diagram resembles letter Z. 6 says named after letter Z, which is a consequence of resemblance. Are they equivalent? The proposition "z-scheme named after letter Z" vs "redox diagram resembles letter Z". The subject differs: 6 subject is z-scheme (diagram). 7 subject is redox diagram from P680 to P700 (which is same diagram). So they refer to same diagram. The relation differs: "named after" vs "resembles". Are they equivalent? Not exactly; one states naming relation, other states visual resemblance. Could be both true but not logically equivalent. The test: could one be true while other false? Yes, a diagram could be named after Z without resembling Z (unlikely but possible). So separate groups.

Thus group 7,17,26 together? 7 and 17 are same relation "resembles". 26 also "resembles" with qualifiers start/end. The qualifiers add extra info (start point P680, end point P700). Does that change proposition? The base claim is still that the diagram resembles letter Z; qualifiers give more specifics but not change core claim. Are they equivalent? The extra qualifiers are additional info, not contradictory. The rule: extra qualifiers that are redundant? Here they specify start/end points, which are already implied by the diagram identity. The core claim same. Since qualifiers add info but not restrict, they still convey all substantive info of others? The others lack qualifiers, but the one with qualifiers includes extra info; does that make it a stronger claim? It adds that the diagram's start and end points are P680 and P700. That is additional info not present in others. The equivalence test requires each member must convey all substantive information of every other member. The one with qualifiers conveys extra info; does it still convey the info of the others? Yes, it says it resembles letter Z (implied). The qualifiers are extra but not contradictory. However the rule says "If one assertion has extra restriction, not equivalent." Here qualifiers are not restrictions but descriptive. They are not restricting the claim; they just add details. Likely still considered equivalent. I'd group 7,17,26 together.

12: energy used to reduce electron transport chain. 20: energy used to reduce chain of electron acceptors. Are they same? 12 object is "electron transport chain". 20 object "chain of electron acceptors". Since those are same entity (named). So they are equivalent. Both say energy used to reduce that chain. So group 12 and 20.

payload.title: Light-dependent reactions
payload.paragraph_text: The photosynthesis process in chloroplasts begins when an electron of P680 of PSII attains a higher - energy level. This energy is used to reduce a chain of electron acceptors that have subsequently lowered redox - potentials. This chain of electron acceptors is known as an electron transport chain. When this chain reaches PS I, an electron is again excited, creating a high redox - potential. The electron transport chain of photosynthesis is often put in a diagram called the z - scheme, because the redox diagram from P680 to P700 resembles the letter z.
